reasons: 화풍: 윤곽이 근흑(재질 어두운 톤 아님) (3/4)

surfaces.part: stone floor slab with flagstone pattern (horizontal surface seen from above)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain block with two zones. Rows 16-47 are a vertical brick wall face with staggered brick courses. Rows 48-49 are a darker shadow strip where the wall meets the floor. Rows 49-110 are a large flagstone floor drawn as a horizontal surface seen from above, with a rune circle in the middle. The rune circle is decor. The floor is foreshortened, its tile rows are spaced evenly, and there is no side face. The wall gives a front face of well over 3 rows, so the block reads as a 3/4-view floor with a back wall.

styleAnswer.evidence: The floor bricks and wall courses are cleanly drawn and carry some per-brick speckle. The gold-ringed rune is a nice accent. But the main stone ramp has only about 4 steps (light, mid, joint, dark speckle), against about 6 in the Beodeul paving. Visible tones per tile are 6, close to the paving's 7 but well above the grass's 3, so that fact alone does not fail it. The near-flat coverage is 32%, while both references are at 0%. It comes from the large flat near-black void margin around the patch and from the plain wall and brick faces. All dark edge pixels are neutral (100%, against 80% for the paving). The mortar and joint lines read as neutral grey and black rather than a dark tint of the stone, so the outline is mixed leaning near_black. Overall it looks slightly flatter and more sticker-like than the reference paving, where every stone is shaded individually.

answer.evidence: This is a terrain tile. A brick wall face fills rows 14-47 and ends in a dark base shadow at rows 46-47. Below it, rows 48-126 show a large horizontal paved floor seen from above, with a rune circle sitting on it as decor. The wall is a vertical front face of about 34 rows and the floor is the top surface, so the tile reads as a wall and floor pair in 3/4 view. The dark outer border is not a part of the object.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 6 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference, so on the tone count it is close. The structure is shallower than the reference. The brick wall and the floor flagstones each use about 3-4 grey steps: a mid grey, a lighter top edge, and darker mortar lines. The reference paving carries about 6 steps, with per-stone shading and grain. Flat coverage is 32% against 0% in both references, so large areas of the flagstones and the wall are single-colour fill with only sparse speckle dots. The measured dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, and the picture agrees: the outline is a neutral near-black/dark navy rim and the mortar lines are neutral grey, with no tint from the neighbouring material. This is the sticker look. The reference paving is itself 80% neutral, but the grass reference is tinted. The glowing rune medallion is a clean, well-made accent, but it does not make up for the flat stone surfaces. Overall it is a tidy but flatter and shallower ground patch than the Beodeul standard.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone-brick floor with a dark back wall and a central rune circle. Each tile shows about 6 visible tones, close to the paving reference's 7. Bricks are regular, with only 3-4 lightness steps on the stone ramp (light edge, mid, dark mortar) and sparse speckle. The reference paving has more irregular, one-by-one shaded stones with tinted highlights and no flat blocks, while the candidate has 32% near-flat coverage against the reference's 0%. The back wall and the grey brick faces are large areas of uniform grey with little grain. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the dark border and mortar read as a neutral black sticker-like line rather than a tinted dark material tone; the reference paving is at 80%, so it is not much better on this measure. Overall it is tidy but shallower and more uniform than the Beodeul standard.
